messages.author: 6a288128bce8283d
messages.subject: Spatial dependency/correlation in residuals
parts:
Hello all,

I am trying to see if there is a spatial signal left over in the occu
model residuals. In the unmarkedFit.R file I have seen that you
basically use:

y <- getY(object@data)
e <- fitted(object, na.rm = FALSE)
r <- y - e

As this will result in residual values for each of the observations
and not just for each site I was wondering how you usually test for
spatial correlation in the residuals?

For the initial test of spatial autocorrelation I used the naive
column of the following table:

site visit1 visit2 visit3 naive
1 0 1 0 0.333
2 1 1 1 1
3 0 1 1 0.6666

Do you think that is correct or would you use a different way?

Thank you very much for your help,
Richard

messages.author: 681fb59733e01a1e
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Spatial dependency/correlation in residuals
parts:
Hi Richard, as far as I know, there is no theory or methodology available to do what you're asking. There are a number of interesting research problems apparent.
My recommendation would be to pursue fitting autologistic models using WinBUGS or other software for such purposes.
regards
andy

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Spatial dependency/correlation in residuals
parts:
hi Richard,
To clarify my previous comment: I think the basic structure of the
problem suggests that you are interested in spatial dependence in the
latent occupancy state. While the model provides estimates of
occupancy (or occupancy state), the only residuals you can compute
apply to the expected observations and those are not binary
observations so standard measures of dependence for binary state
variables can't be computed.
A number of ad hoc approaches to the problem are evident but nothing
that is apprently straightforward in unmarked.

My suggestion previously was to think about directly modeling the
dependence in the state variable which can be done using autologistic
models for the state variable. (but not in unmarked).

regards
andy

Hi Andy,

Thanks again.
Do you write about this in your book by any chance (I just picked up a
copy from the library)?

If I understand you correctly, I could use the autologistic model to
adjust the occupancy estimates?

What I have recently seen was: "To assess the degree of spatial
autocorrelation in response
variables not accounted for by predictor variables, we calculated
Moran’s I (R version 2.0.1)
for residuals from occupancy models across a set of distance
categories" (Moore & Swihart 2005)
They used the occupancy model from the MacKenzie et al. (2002) paper
with MARK, which is why I thought it might
be possible to do something similar from the unmarked output.

Regards,
Richard

messages.author: 4a15de51da4445ae
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Spatial dependency/correlation in residuals
parts:
hi Richard,
we just briefly touch on autologistic models in the book (chapter 9 I
think) - but, yes, my point is that you should just build in a spatial
dependence effect by expression logit(psi[i]) to be a function of how
many neighboring sites are occupied.
Re: Moran's I and related things -- I think the issue is that you're
not producing predictions of the spatially correlated variable but,
rather, predictions of the observations. The estimates of spatial
dependence from those predictions will be, I think, very biased
(towards 0) and probably meaningless in practical sample sizes.
It would be easy enough to evaluate this by simulation I guess....
regards
andy

messages.author: 9548b9e0c8258268
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Spatial dependency/correlation in residuals
parts:
Richard,

Along the lines of Andy's point that psi_i is the modeling level wherein spatial autocorrelation should be included, there are other techniques you can try for exploratory data analysis at that level before building a full model.  For example, you can fit the independent model (e.g., with unmarked).  And then instead of looking at observation residuals, you can compute E(Z_i | Y_i) at each site using Baye's rule and use this as an estimate of occupancy.  Then you can compute Moran's I on the pseudo occupancy residuals:  E(Z_i | Y_i) - psi_i.

Just keep in mind that this is still a hack useful mainly for EDA and not for a final analysis.  Andy's suggestion of fitting a full autologistic model is more appropriate for the final analysis should you decide to include spatial autocorrelation.

Ian

Hi Ian,

For independent model do you mean

lm1 <- occu( ~1 ~1, UMF)

and then for compute E(Z_i | Y_i)

predict(lm1, type='state')

?

This would result in a psi that is the same for all sites.
And from there I could the pseudo residuals with my 'loaded' model
estimates.

Thanks,
Richard

On Nov 4, 6:53 pm, Ian Fiske <ianfi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Richard,
>
> Along the lines of Andy's point that psi_i is the modeling level wherein
> spatial autocorrelation should be included, there are other techniques you
> can try for exploratory data analysis at that level before building a full
> model.  For example, you can fit the independent model (e.g., with
> unmarked).  And then instead of looking at observation residuals, you can
> compute E(Z_i | Y_i) at each site using Baye's rule and use this as an
> estimate of occupancy.  Then you can compute Moran's I on the pseudo
> occupancy residuals:  E(Z_i | Y_i) - psi_i.
>
> Just keep in mind that this is still a hack useful mainly for EDA and not
> for a final analysis.  Andy's suggestion of fitting a full autologistic
> model is more appropriate for the final analysis should you decide to
> include spatial autocorrelation.
>
> Ian
>

> On Thu, Nov 4, 2010 at 9:20 PM, Jeffrey Royle <jaro...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > hi Richard,
